observations.code_quote:
"description": "Turn a feature flag on. Requires the flag's numeric ID; use `feature-flag-get-definition-by-key` to get it from a key, or `feature-flag-get-all` to search by key or name.

Sets `active` to true and changes nothing else. This tool never accepts or replaces the `filters` object, so targeting, rollout percentages, variants and payloads cannot change. To change who the flag is served to, use `update-feature-flag`.

Pass `version` from the flag you read. A flag whose `filters.version` is 2 requires it, so read the flag first and send its current `version`; never guess it. When the call would change the flag, a stale `version` returns 409: read the flag again and decide against its current state. A call that changes nothing succeeds without checking `version`, and the response carries the current `version`.

Returns 400 when the flag is archived (call `feature-flag-unarchive` first), when a flag it depends on is disabled, or when a release condition targets a deleted cohort (remove that condition with `update-feature-flag`). Returns 409 when an approval policy gates enabling. Enabling an already-enabled flag succeeds and changes nothing, so retrying is safe.

`feature-flag-get-definition-by-key` also finds archived flags. `feature-flag-get-all` hides archived flags unless you pass `{"archived":"true"}`.

To turn the flag on at a future time instead, use `scheduled-changes-create` with the `update_status` operation.",

observations.code_quote:
"description": "Update a feature flag by numeric ID (partial update: only the fields you include are changed). Use this for edits that have no dedicated tool, such as property filters, adding and removing release conditions, variant definitions, payloads, tags and the description.

Prefer a dedicated tool whenever the request matches one. `feature-flag-enable`, `feature-flag-disable`, `feature-flag-archive` and `feature-flag-unarchive` each change one state field and send no `filters`. A targeting change someone else made between your read and your write is therefore not overwritten. Send `active` or `archived` here only when the same request also changes targeting or another field, so the whole edit lands in one write.

`feature-flag-set-release-condition-rollout` changes one release condition's percentage and `feature-flag-roll-out-to-everyone` serves the flag to its whole audience. Both send no `filters` and both refuse the write when the flag changed after the version you read, so a concurrent edit cannot be lost. On a flag without `filters.version` 2, this tool does not check `version`, so it writes even when the flag changed after your read. It replaces the whole `filters` object with your copy of it. Use it for a rollout change only when those two tools cannot express it, such as changing the split between variants while leaving the audience alone.

A flag whose `filters.version` is 2 requires `version` for any change, so read the flag first and send its current `version`; never guess it. A stale `version` returns 409: read the flag again and decide against its current state. Don't send `filters` for such a flag: its rules change through `feature-flag-rules-update`.

Rollout conditions, variants, and payloads live in the structured `filters` param, and sending `filters` replaces the whole object, so read the flag first and merge your change. Each release condition you read has a `condition_id`. Send it unchanged on every condition you keep, edit, or move, and leave it off a new condition. A `condition_id` belongs to the flag you read it from, so leave it off a condition copied from a different flag. Once any condition has a `condition_id`, a condition without one is treated as new. This tool uses the ID to restore each condition's property types and targeting, so a reorder, deletion, or edit keeps every condition on the persons or group type it targeted. If a `condition_id` matches no condition on the flag, the flag may have changed after your read, and the update is refused. Read the flag again and rebuild the update. When the flag targets groups, keep `type: "group"`, `group_type_index`, and `filters.aggregation_group_type_index` in what you send; if you omit them this tool restores them from the existing flag so group targeting is not silently converted to person targeting. When the flag's conditions don't all target the same thing (some target persons and others a group type, or they target different group types), set `aggregation_group_type_index` on every new condition. Use null for persons. If you send no `condition_id` values, set `aggregation_group_type_index` on every condition whenever you add, remove, reorder, or change the properties of conditions. Otherwise this tool can't tell which target each condition keeps, and it refuses the update. Use `feature-flag-get-definition-by-key` when you have the string key: it returns the numeric ID and the full definition in one call. Use `feature-flag-get-definition` when you already have the ID. To apply a change at a future time instead, use `scheduled-changes-create`.",
